docs.title: Know your Linux attack surface.
docs.text:
Your field guide to exposed services, permissions and runtime evidence. Start with one Linux system. Follow a finding back to its source. Understand what was checked and where visibility was limited.

Run your first scan Explore LASA

docs.title: From a local snapshot to a clear next step
docs.text:
• 1. Check your system

    Install LASA on Linux AMD64 or ARM64. Use lasa doctor to check platform support and the visibility available to your current user.

  • 2. Understand the evidence

    Run a read-only scan. Connect process, socket, namespace, mount and permission metadata to findings, and review any collection gaps.

  • 3. Review and follow through

    Trace each finding to its evidence. Review recommended remediation, make changes through your own operations process, and scan again.

docs.title: Choose your next step
docs.text:
• I am new to LASA

    Install with your Linux package manager, Linux Homebrew or a verified release binary, and complete your first scan.

  • I want to automate scans

    Choose scan options, export formats and exit codes for your workflow.

  • I am investigating a finding

    Read severity and supporting evidence, assess uncertainty and review your next steps.

  • I need to understand data access

    See exactly what LASA reads, what it stores and which permissions it needs.

  • I operate Linux systems

    Schedule scans, manage report retention and configure the optional systemd service.

  • I need to resolve a problem

    Understand permission errors, incomplete collection and diagnostic messages.

docs.title: Inspect the configurations that matter
docs.text:
Connect effective service settings, local identities, execution paths and optional vendor advisory data to findings. Choose security inspection modules, review their data access, and understand detection coverage before enabling them.

lasa scan --inspect systemd,ssh,permissions

docs.title: Your first scan
docs.text:
After installing LASA, check your system and collect a snapshot:

lasa doctor
lasa scan

Save the evidence as JSON and create a self-contained HTML report for review:

lasa scan --format json --output first.report.json
lasa report --input first.report.json --format html --output first.report.html

docs.title: Know what your results prove
docs.text:
LASA reads local Linux metadata and evaluates it with local security rules. Optional inspections add the explicitly selected configuration providers. It does not exploit the host, modify security configuration, capture network payloads or upload reports. Your reports stay on your system, with no telemetry or cloud account required.

An empty findings list does not establish that a system is secure. Check the scan scope and collection diagnostics before drawing conclusions. See compatibility and limits and collection, access and privacy for the boundaries of a scan.

docs.title: Versions and compatibility
docs.text: Run lasa version to check the installed scanner version. Executable versions and report schema versions are separate; see understand results when comparing reports across releases.

docs.title: Conventions and global options
docs.text:
Run lasa --help or lasa COMMAND --help for help generated from the implementation. --diagnostics-format text|json controls fatal command diagnostics on stderr. When an output format is selected, stdout contains that output only. If --output is provided, the report is written privately to that path instead of stdout.

Shell completion is built in:

lasa completion bash > lasa-completion.bash
lasa version

docs.title: lasa scan
docs.text:
lasa scan --profile standard --timeout 30s
lasa scan --format json --output host.report.json --strict
lasa scan --format sarif --output host.sarif --fail-on high
Flag Default Meaning --profile standard standard, deep, container, sensor --timeout 30s Cooperative collection deadline, 1ms through 24h --workers 4 Process collection workers, 1–32 --max-processes 4096 Visible PID inspection budget, maximum 65,536 --max-fds 512 Descriptors inspected per PID, maximum 65,536 --max-files 4096 File metadata budget, maximum 100,000 --roots See privacy guide Comma-separated explicit metadata roots, replaces defaults --sensor-duration 3s Optional event window, 1ms–10m, only used by sensor profile --inspect none Opt-in modules or all; see security inspections --ssh-context root/localhost context Repeatable effective SSH context --network-source / --network-destination none IP literals for local nftables modeling --network-interface none Ingress interface for modeled packet --container-socket /run/docker.sock Explicit Docker-compatible UNIX endpoint --advisories none Local release-specific advisory database --advisory-max-age 168h Additional cache age limit; own expiry always applies --max-inspection-items 256 Per-module work budget, 1–4096 --inspection-command-timeout 5s Each native-provider deadline, 1ms–1m --format terminal terminal, json, html, sarif --output stdout Atomic private destination; existing regular files are replaced --rules none Explicit additional local YAML rule pack; builtin IDs cannot be overridden --suppressions none Explicit versioned local JSON suppression file --strict false Incomplete collection yields exit 3 after report output --fail-on disabled Unsuppressed severity threshold: informational, low, medium, high, critical

Timeouts are cooperative, checked between bounded operations. A blocked kernel or remote-filesystem syscall may not return immediately at the deadline. Root /, traversal paths, unnormalized roots and more than 128 roots are rejected. Other fixed internal budgets bound namespaces, tables, graph edges, rule size and report input; hitting them produces a diagnostic.

docs.title: Exit codes
lasa doctor
docs.text:
lasa doctor
lasa doctor --format json

Checks Linux compatibility, the scanner's own procfs/security/socket/mount access and optional BTF/tracepoint visibility. Optional failures do not prevent the static prerequisite result from succeeding. Doctor does not prove that all other processes are accessible or that a BPF program can load; the selected sensor performs actual feature probing and attachment.

docs.title: lasa explain <finding-id> --report <path>
docs.text:
lasa explain FULL_FINGERPRINT --report host.report.json
lasa explain FULL_FINGERPRINT --report host.report.json --format json

Uses the full finding fingerprint, not the rule ID. Shows the stored finding, its evidence and the matching recorded evaluation. It does not rescan or test exploitability. A missing fingerprint produces FINDING_NOT_FOUND. JSON output uses lasa.explanation/v1.

docs.title: lasa diff <previous-report> <current-report>
docs.text: Produces JSON with new, continuing, changed, resolved and unknown categories. Different host identities are rejected. Unavailable assets, changed profile, incomplete collection or a missing explicit negative evaluation keep old findings in unknown. LASA deliberately favors uncertainty over a false resolution claim.

docs.title: lasa report --input <path> --format <format>
docs.text:
lasa report --input host.report.json --format html --output host.report.html
lasa report --input host.report.json --format sarif --output host.sarif

Renders without contacting or inspecting the scanned host. Inputs are capped at 64MiB, must be regular files, must use the supported report schema and must preserve valid evidence references. Unknown JSON fields are rejected for this schema version.

docs.title: lasa rules list
docs.text: --format terminal|json lists builtin rule versions, categories, conditions and remediation. --rules PATH appends an explicit local pack for inspection. No rule pack is downloaded automatically and no shell/expression code is executed from rules. See the maintainer authoring guide if you operate custom packs.

docs.title: lasa daemon
docs.text:
The scan flags for profile, timeout and resource scope apply. Additional flags:

Flag Default Meaning --state-dir ~/.local/state/lasa, or ./lasa-state if home lookup fails Private state directory and exclusive daemon lock --interval 15m Delay after a completed snapshot, minimum 1s --retention 96 Retained LASA snapshot count, 1–10,000 --rules none Local additional rule pack, loaded at startup --suppressions none Suppression policy, loaded at startup 
lasa daemon --state-dir ./private-state --interval 15m --retention 96

The daemon runs scans sequentially, persists one JSON report at a time and logs snapshot status to stderr. It does not overlap scans or make remote API calls. Stop with SIGINT or SIGTERM; allow the in-progress scan and bounded filesystem operations time to finish. Persistence, retention or fatal scan failures terminate the daemon with a diagnostic so a supervisor can alert and restart it.

docs.title: lasa advisories
docs.text:
lasa advisories update --release trixie --output advisories.json
lasa advisories import --input authenticated-vendor.json --output advisories.json

Update is an explicit verified-HTTPS download from the official Debian tracker. Import validates a local lasa.advisories/v1 file; it does not authenticate arbitrary claimed provenance. Both write private atomic files and leave the prior output intact on validation/download failure. See package advisories.

docs.title: Additional daemon limits
docs.text: --retention-bytes defaults to 0 (disabled) and limits managed snapshot bytes in addition to the count limit. --min-free-bytes defaults to 16,777,216 (16MiB) and reserves free space after the next report. The free-space check is advisory; a concurrent writer can still cause an atomic-write failure. A newest snapshot larger than its quota produces an error rather than silently deleting every report. Inspection flags have the same meaning in scan and daemon.

docs.title: Platform targets
docs.text:
LASA targets Linux AMD64 and ARM64 little-endian systems. Native macOS and Windows scans are unsupported. Build the Linux binaries from a suitable Linux toolchain and use real Linux hosts/VMs for kernel-sensitive testing. ARM64 cross-compilation alone does not validate an ARM64 kernel at runtime.

openat2, procfs, visible namespaces and permission-compatible metadata access are required for the intended static workflow. Kernels predating openat2, hardened syscall filters and procfs restrictions can prevent collection. No insecure path-following fallback is used. The scanner reports failures rather than pretending that a version string establishes compatibility.

Static collection and report workflows were exercised on a Debian 13.6 AMD64 cloud host. Both target architectures have reproducible build checks. Privileged eBPF attachment/event delivery, the full host/container namespace matrix and live systemd deployment still require target-host validation. CI configuration is a plan for repeatable checks; an unexecuted CI job is not a verified compatibility claim.

docs.title: Capability matrix
docs.text: Capability Current behavior Real process/identity/namespace metadata Implemented, bounded and permission-aware TCP/UDP IPv4/IPv6 and UNIX endpoints Implemented for enumerated process network namespaces Interface addresses and routing Scanner network namespace; no upstream topology guarantee Scoped file metadata, ACL presence, file capability xattrs Implemented; effective access evaluation is conservative Cgroup runtime and service association Heuristic association, not a runtime API inventory Kernel hardening metadata Selected allowlist; not a complete kernel or LSM policy audit Evidence-linked local correlations Implemented; conditional compromise remains explicit 33 builtin rule definitions Baseline and opt-in inspection rules; external-confirmation rules still require an independent source Active external exposure validation Not implemented; no active port scanning Continuous runtime monitoring Not implemented; optional bounded observation windows are supported Optional eBPF Compiled CO-RE object and feature-detecting loader; runtime support requires target-host validation Identity-aware discretionary access Optional local-account/ACL/traversal analysis; LSM, immutable flags and external identity policy remain qualified Remote/cloud host inventory Not implemented or required SecureObs upload No built-in upload; local versioned ingestion contract provided

docs.title: Namespace and container boundaries
docs.text:
Process IDs are scoped. Process identity includes boot identity, PID namespace and start time, so reuse of a numeric PID does not imply the same process. The scanner never treats a capability mask in an arbitrary user namespace as proof of host-level privilege.

A process can be visible while its descriptors, executable or namespace links are restricted. Network namespaces are inspected through visible process representatives; hidden processes and namespace objects with no visible representative may remain unobserved. Only the scanner namespace's interface API is queried; other namespaces' full interface topology is not inferred from their socket tables.

Container detection uses cgroup naming hints. Custom runtimes, altered cgroup layouts and ambiguous host-style mount names can defeat or confuse those hints. Reports qualify them. A container profile acknowledges limited visibility; it does not grant access or escape the container.

docs.title: Filesystem and service boundaries
docs.text:
The default scope omits arbitrary homes, deep directory trees, hidden service paths and symlink targets. Scoped metadata is not proof a service will load a file. Sudo/SSH acceptance policies, systemd activation, ACL interpretation, supplementary-group membership and mount/execution options can affect impact.

The default scan does not read service configuration contents or process environments. Optional inspections add effective native service/SSH/sudo policy, selected cron configuration, local identities, runtime settings and package data. See security inspections and data access for exact sources and retained fields. Kernel LSM presence remains contextual evidence, not proof of a policy's effectiveness.

docs.title: Completeness, scoring and exploitability
docs.text: No scan provides complete host security coverage or guaranteed detection. Scores are prioritization values, not exploit probabilities. A high-confidence observation of a risky combination does not prove a successful compromise. The supported static workflow can be useful while collection is partial; strict mode and downstream acceptance policy determine whether that coverage meets your operational needs.

docs.title: Inspection provider requirements
docs.text:
Module Provider/requirements Explicit boundaries systemd/timers Trusted root-owned systemctl, system manager access, JSON inventory output and selected effective properties Alternate roots, unsupported execution flags, unresolved command syntax and inaccessible managers remain unknown SSH Trusted root-owned OpenSSH sshd 9.3+ with configuration-only -G, readable configuration Older provider versions remain unsupported; no fallback to host-key validation sudo Trusted native sudo with supported long-list policy output; authorization for noninteractive queries External identities, unusual RunAs/output syntax and query denials remain explicit gaps permissions Local passwd/group records, metadata/ACL access, supported openat2 behavior and mount metadata No arbitrary NSS membership reconstruction, mandatory-policy proof, write attempt or universal remote-filesystem authorization model firewall Trusted nft, authorized ruleset access in the scanner network namespace Supported nftables subset only; named sets, transformations, other hooks and external filtering can make verdicts unknown containers Explicit Docker-compatible local UNIX API 1.24–1.50 No native containerd gRPC, Kubernetes inventory or remote TCP API packages Trusted dpkg-query or rpm, exact-release advisory data and native version semantics Automatic feed retrieval targets Debian; other supported schemes require authenticated database import scheduler Readable supported cron/root spool sources; systemd manager for timer checks Complex shell programs, wrappers, anacron semantics and arbitrary startup mechanisms are not fully interpreted

The scratch container image intentionally contains no host administration tools. Installing or mounting a native tool alone does not establish host visibility; manager sockets, namespaces, identity mapping and filesystem scope must also be correct. The scanner refuses tools with writable or non-root-controlled executable ancestry. Do not weaken these checks to remove diagnostics.

Fixture and contract tests establish parser/rule behavior. Native provider, kernel and architecture compatibility must also be validated on the deployment targets. The maintainer VM harness automates that work from macOS or an authorized disposable Linux VM; an unexecuted matrix is not a verified support claim.

docs.title: Package format availability
docs.text:
Native DEB/APT, RPM/DNF/YUM/Zypper, Arch/Pacman and Alpine/APK repositories target Linux AMD64 and ARM64. Linux Homebrew and verified archives remain available deployment methods. Repository configuration is required before a stock package manager recognizes LASA. Formats do not imply default-distribution inclusion or support for every historical kernel/derivative.

Packaging/protocol validation and scanner runtime validation are separate. Representative native package clients run in isolated container tests; full kernel/provider behavior requires the deployment-target matrix above. ARM64 cross-compilation and metadata verification do not substitute for native ARM64 kernel/provider testing. See installation.

docs.title: Data collection contract
docs.text:
The default scan reads local Linux metadata through a fixed set of collectors. Optional --inspect modules expand the collection contract explicitly, as described below. It does not recursively search the entire disk by default. Explicit roots expand only filesystem metadata scope, not permission to read their file contents.

Source Data read Purpose and what appears in a report /proc/PID/stat PID, parent PID, start time; bounded parsing of kernel fields Process identity and PID-reuse protection; no full command arguments /proc/PID/status Command name, UIDs/GIDs, groups, capability masks, seccomp, NoNewPrivs Privilege and isolation context /proc/PID/exe Kernel link plus pinned executable device/inode metadata Executable identity and file correlation; no executable bytes /proc/PID/ns/* Namespace link identities Scope and namespace relationships /proc/PID/uid_map, gid_map Namespace mapping ranges Interpret credentials and capability context /proc/PID/cgroup Cgroup membership paths with long hexadecimal identifiers pseudonymized Runtime hints, service association and stable context /proc/PID/fd/* Link metadata, bounded descriptor count Socket inode ownership; descriptor contents are never opened /proc/PID/net/tcp*, udp*, unix Bounded socket table rows in visible network namespaces Endpoints, listener/bound state, UNIX paths and owners Scanner namespace interface API and route tables Interface addresses, flags, names, IPv4/IPv6 route metadata Local topology evidence; not upstream firewall or NAT knowledge /proc/PID/mountinfo Mount roots/targets, filesystem, options and propagation fields Namespace-scoped mounts and read-only context Scoped file paths Device/inode, ownership, mode, capability/ACL xattr metadata Unsafe permission candidates and privileged-executable association Selected /proc/sys and /sys paths Ptrace, disclosure, namespace and BPF restrictions; LSM/lockdown and cgroup indicators Kernel posture context and explicit collection gaps /etc/machine-id or fallback Machine identity, hashed before reporting Cross-scan host mapping; raw machine ID is not retained Boot ID, kernel release, OS release metadata Boot context, architecture, distribution Process identity, compatibility and scan context Optional eBPF Bounded process name/identity, endpoint metadata, selected syscall event outcomes and namespace flags Finite runtime observation; no traffic payloads

The scanner's own procfs file-descriptor links can be used to address a pinned file for metadata/xattr inspection. This does not grant permission to read the scanned application's contents.

docs.title: Default filesystem roots
docs.text:
/usr/bin
/usr/sbin
/usr/local/bin
/etc/systemd/system
/usr/lib/systemd/system
/etc/sudoers
/etc/sudoers.d
/etc/ssh
/root/.ssh
/run/docker.sock
/run/containerd/containerd.sock

Traversal is bounded to two directory levels under each root, a global entry budget and a deadline. Symlinks are excluded, including ordinary distribution alternatives links. A parent symlink can also make an explicit root inaccessible; choose its canonical target deliberately instead of expecting automatic traversal. User home directories are not recursively enumerated. Add a specific authorized-key directory only when it is part of the intended scope.

docs.title: Optional inspection access
docs.text:
Enable these sources only through the corresponding --inspect module. Their scope is independent of --roots. The default scan does not query them.

Module/source Data accessed Retained data Local /etc/passwd and /etc/group Account/group records, including fields that must be discarded Selected names, numeric IDs and group relationships needed for findings; password/GECOS fields are discarded Systemd system manager Loaded/enabled service inventory and selected effective service/timer properties Unit identity/state, selected settings, executable/script/environment-file paths and supporting permission metadata Configuration-only sshd -G -C Native SSH configuration resolution, including configured includes and the chosen connection context Selected effective authentication/permission settings and the recorded context; LASA does not request host-key validation Native sudo -n -ll -U Effective policy provider output for local identities Selected root grants and command paths; general policy text is discarded Explicit execution/configuration paths Metadata and ACLs along supported path resolutions, including normal symlink targets Named discretionary writer candidates and selected component metadata; target file contents are not opened by LASA Native nftables query JSON ruleset in the scanner network namespace A supported-model verdict and packet context; no packet payloads or active probe Selected Docker-compatible UNIX socket Version, container inventory and container inspect responses through GET requests Selected privilege, namespace, mount, capability and confinement settings; container IDs are pseudonymized Native package database and ownership queries Installed package/source versions and selected executable ownership Inventory count, advisory-relevant versions and selected process relationships Explicit local advisory file Vendor-derived advisory ranges and source/freshness metadata Relevant advisory identifiers, fixed versions, severity and provenance; not the entire cache Cron/root spool files and systemd timers Supported schedules and command configuration Source/line identity, selected execution/search paths, user and permissions; command arguments and unrelated environment values are discarded

Native systemd properties and runtime inspect responses can include command arguments, environment values, labels or other sensitive fields in transient memory. LASA selects the fields above and does not persist raw responses, full command arguments, environment dumps or raw configuration files. This is a broader access choice than metadata-only scanning; it is not a promise that sensitive fields never enter memory.

Native tools and local management daemons are trusted parts of the inspected system. Their configured includes, identity providers and ordinary audit logging follow host policy. A native sudo/NSS lookup can contact an organization identity service; a read-only management query can cause ordinary daemon/audit logging. LASA does not change enforcement settings or execute remediation. It does not request Docker mutations, remote runtime endpoints or host-key validation.

docs.title: What LASA does not collect or do
docs.text:
• The default scan does not read /proc/PID/environ, full argv/cmdline, credential-store/private-key contents, application logs or arbitrary application contents. Optional inspection access and transient native/API data are described above. LASA does not directly request /etc/shadow, private-key bodies or /proc/PID/environ.
  • No network payloads, packet capture, authentication attempts, active vulnerability probes or exploitation.
  • No runtime API requests or control-socket connection for baseline analysis. Only the explicit containers module uses its selected Docker-compatible endpoint.
  • No automatic remediation, host policy modification, privilege escalation or installation-time kernel enforcement.
  • No remote telemetry, report upload or SecureObs authentication. Scans make no direct outbound IP advisory/API requests. lasa advisories update is a separate explicit HTTPS download; native identity-provider behavior follows host policy.

Metadata can still be sensitive. Executable paths, process names, UNIX socket paths, interfaces, mount paths, identity numbers and service names reveal system structure. A command name can itself contain a sensitive string chosen by its owner. Omitting arguments and hashing selected identifiers is not a guarantee of anonymity. Review report handling under your own data classification policy.

docs.title: What is stored
docs.text:
A one-shot terminal scan does not create a hidden report database. --output stores the selected report. JSON schema v2 retains the complete snapshot, enabled inspection modules, requested metadata roots, scope fingerprint and inspection assets: metadata entities, observations, provenance graph, findings, evaluation outcomes, coverage, diagnostics and optional runtime events/drop counts. HTML retains a readable representation of evidence, findings and errors. SARIF retains finding-level information and stable fingerprints.

The daemon creates a private state directory, an exclusive lock file and timestamped JSON snapshots. Retention is bounded by snapshot count and an optional --retention-bytes quota for managed snapshots. It is not time-based retention or a quota on unrelated files. The daemon also checks a configured free-space reserve before persisting a report. Only scanner-named regular snapshot files owned by the daemon user are retention candidates. Unrelated files and symlinks are not deleted. Temporary files from interrupted writes are not treated as reports or automatically interpreted.

docs.title: Permissions and exposure
docs.text:
New output files use mode 0600; newly created state directories use 0700. Report writes use an exclusive temporary file, sync and atomic rename. Symlink paths and non-regular output targets are rejected. These protections do not defend against a compromised root user, a hostile kernel or a user who subsequently copies a report into a public location.

Terminal rendering escapes control characters. HTML uses escaped output and no remote resources. JSON must be treated as untrusted input by every downstream renderer. A stable fingerprint is a correlation identifier, not an authentication signature or an encryption mechanism.

docs.title: Retention, deletion and export
docs.text: Operators own all stored reports and decide backups, encryption at rest, access control, deletion and export. LASA does not encrypt report files itself. Deleting a report does not delete backups or guarantee physical media erasure. If an external integration is added, obtain authorization, establish transport and storage controls and preserve the report's coverage and uncertainty semantics.

docs.title: Detection coverage
docs.text: LASA prioritizes combinations supported by local evidence. It separates an observed condition, a conditional consequence and information it could not establish. Findings are not proof of exploitation, and a scan with no findings is not a security certification.

docs.title: Detection areas
docs.text:
The builtin catalog contains 33 versioned rule definitions. Available findings depend on enabled modules, permissions, supported providers and evidence coverage.

Area What LASA helps investigate Exposed services Non-loopback listeners combined with privilege, capabilities or conventional management ports. Isolation and containers Selected namespace/capability combinations; runtime-confirmed privileged settings, sensitive mounts and control-socket exposure when runtime inspection is enabled. Privileged execution Unsafe metadata on privileged executables, system search paths and service launch files; named discretionary writer candidates from optional identity/ACL analysis. Access and authentication Sensitive sudo/SSH path permissions; effective SSH policy for recorded contexts; selected effective sudo root grants. Service and scheduled execution Supported root-service, cron and timer execution paths that local identities can influence. Package advisories Release-specific affected package ranges, high-severity vendor assessments and selected running-listener associations. Local firewall context Supported nftables decisions for a recorded new-connection packet.

The separately confirmed external-exposure rule remains unavailable to purely local static scans. LASA does not invent an external confirmation source to make that rule trigger.

docs.title: Reading a finding
docs.text:
A finding includes its rule/version, affected subject, severity, confidence, supporting observations, prerequisites, uncertainty and remediation. New inspection findings identify the inspected service, identity, endpoint, package or configuration path. JSON and the HTML evidence table retain the selected settings and permission/advisory details.

An observation can be reliable while its possible consequence remains conditional. For example, native policy can establish a root delegation grant without establishing that the account is compromised. A discretionary writer candidate does not prove that mandatory policy permits an actual modification. An affected package version does not prove that a particular vulnerable function is reachable.

Scores prioritize review. They are not probabilities of compromise. Review network scope, identity, activation and compensating controls before making operational changes.

docs.title: Collection outcomes
docs.text:
Review collector coverage and individual diagnostics. unknown is distinct from a negative observation, and not_applicable is distinct from secure. Collector completeness applies to its declared bounded scope, not every asset or security control on the host.

Optional inspections appear as inspect.systemd, inspect.ssh, and similarly named coverage entries. Counts describe enumerated work; diagnostics can also describe unavailable prerequisites. They are not a percentage of total host security coverage.

docs.title: Changes and remediation tracking
docs.text:
lasa diff before.report.json after.report.json

The diff distinguishes new, continuing, changed, resolved and unknown findings. Changes in supporting evidence can move a continuing finding into changed, even if severity is unchanged.

A finding can be resolved only when the corresponding evaluation establishes absence or non-applicability, its relevant evidence collectors have complete coverage, and the declared scan scope is compatible. Losing access, narrowing roots, disabling a module or changing an SSH context must not silently resolve an issue. An unrelated collector failure can remain visible without blocking an independently verified resolution.

Diff schema v2 also reports observed changes in listeners, process privilege context, file permissions and selected inspected settings. A listener no longer observed is a statement about compared snapshots, not proof it is unreachable everywhere. Process comparisons across boot changes retain uncertainty. Surface changes are bounded and indicate truncation explicitly.

docs.title: Handling intentional exceptions
docs.text:
Use justified, expiring suppressions for intended administrator delegation or accepted configuration risks. Keep evidence and coverage in the retained report. A suppression changes handling; it does not change the observation or prove the risk has disappeared.

See results, security inspections, compatibility and limits, and troubleshooting.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
Use Linux on AMD64 or ARM64. LASA uses openat2 to constrain metadata paths; Linux 5.6 introduced this syscall, but kernel configuration, seccomp and container policy can still make it unavailable. Procfs must be mounted and the scanner's own metadata must be visible. No database, runtime control socket, API key, SecureObs account or outbound network access is required for scanning.

Build with the supported Go 1.27.2 patch release. CGO is disabled for release binaries. A C compiler is needed only for race tests and a pinned Clang/libbpf toolchain only for regenerating the optional eBPF object. The object is already embedded in normal builds.

docs.title: Configure your Linux package manager
docs.text:
LASA publishes its own signed repositories for Linux AMD64 and ARM64. Configure the repository once; subsequent installs and upgrades use your normal package manager. A stock machine does not know LASA's repository until this setup runs.

Download the complete setup script over HTTPS before executing it:

curl --proto '=https' --tlsv1.2 -fsSLo install-lasa.sh https://lasa.secureobs.com/install.sh
sh install-lasa.sh
lasa doctor

Run these commands from a directory you own. The script uses root or sudo for repository/package changes, detects the available manager, verifies the pinned signing key and installs LASA. sh install-lasa.sh --detect prints the selected manager/architecture without configuring a repository. Review the downloaded script according to your organization's policy. Initial trust comes from the HTTPS site and its published key pins; do not bypass signature, checksum or TLS failures.

Linux family Repository / native package Install after setup Update Debian, Ubuntu and compatible derivatives APT / DEB sudo apt install lasa sudo apt update && sudo apt install --only-upgrade lasa Fedora, RHEL, Rocky, AlmaLinux, Oracle Linux, CentOS Stream RPM / DNF sudo dnf install lasa sudo dnf upgrade lasa Compatible systems using YUM RPM / YUM sudo yum install lasa sudo yum update lasa openSUSE / SUSE with compatible RPM support RPM / Zypper sudo zypper install lasa sudo zypper update lasa Arch Linux; compatible Arch Linux ARM targets Pacman sudo pacman -S lasa sudo pacman -Syu Alpine APK sudo apk add lasa sudo apk update && sudo apk upgrade lasa

These are LASA-owned repositories, separate from each distribution's default repositories. A package format being available does not establish kernel/provider compatibility for every derivative or historical release. Use a maintained operating system with the kernel requirements above; then check lasa doctor and compatibility. Gentoo, NixOS and other managers can use reviewed binary/source deployment; no official ebuild, Nixpkgs entry, AUR listing or distribution-maintainer endorsement is implied.

The setup script refuses conflicting existing LASA configuration/key files. It retains the distribution's other repositories. Arch setup performs a full system upgrade before installation, following the rolling-release requirement to avoid partial upgrades. The commands select architecture automatically. Optional systemd units are examples only; no package starts a service, grants scanner privileges or runs a scan.

For APT-only setup, the existing https://lasa.secureobs.com/install-apt.sh remains available. APT uses a repository-specific keyring and signed metadata. RPM repositories require both package and metadata signatures. Pacman verifies database and package signatures. APK packages and indexes use RSA/SHA-256 signatures with a separately pinned Alpine public key.

docs.title: Linux Homebrew
docs.text:
brew install jasonachkar/lasa/lasa
lasa doctor

The formula selects the architecture and verifies an exact archive checksum. Use brew upgrade lasa and brew uninstall lasa.

macOS can manage publishing but cannot run this Linux scanner. The Homebrew formula explicitly requires Linux. Native Windows/WinGet is not supported; WSL users can use their supported Linux distribution's package instructions. No native macOS or Windows security coverage is implied.

docs.title: Remove a package or repository
docs.text:
Use sudo apt remove lasa, sudo dnf remove lasa, sudo yum remove lasa, sudo zypper remove lasa, sudo pacman -R lasa, or sudo apk del lasa. Stop any separately configured daemon first. Package removal retains reports, state and repository configuration.

To stop receiving LASA packages, remove only the LASA-owned entries:

  • APT: /etc/apt/sources.list.d/lasa.list and /usr/share/keyrings/lasa-archive-keyring.gpg.
  • DNF/YUM: /etc/yum.repos.d/lasa.repo; Zypper: /etc/zypp/repos.d/lasa.repo. The public key file is /etc/pki/rpm-gpg/RPM-GPG-KEY-lasa; the imported RPM trust entry is shared RPM state, so review its fingerprint before removing it.
  • Pacman: the Include = /etc/pacman.d/lasa.conf line and /etc/pacman.d/lasa.conf. Remove the specifically identified LASA key through pacman-key only after checking no other repository uses it.
  • APK: the LASA URL line in /etc/apk/repositories and /etc/apk/keys/lasa.rsa.pub.

Do not remove distribution-wide keyrings or unrelated repository files. Local reports and separately installed service units need their own retention/removal policy.

docs.title: Build from source
docs.text:
go version                         # should report go1.27.2
make build
./bin/lasa version
./bin/lasa doctor

Module versions and checksums are pinned in go.mod and go.sum. Installation must preserve module checksum and TLS verification. Do not work around a failed checksum with GOSUMDB=off, an insecure proxy or modified expected digests.

docs.title: Native installation
docs.text:
An administrator may install a reviewed build:

sudo install -m 0755 bin/lasa /usr/local/bin/lasa
lasa doctor
lasa scan

This command installs the binary; the scanner itself never invokes sudo. Do not make the binary SUID or assign broad file capabilities to it. For direct downloads, verify checksums and release provenance before installation.

docs.title: Verify release provenance
docs.text:
GitHub Actions releases carry a GitHub build attestation. Verify the downloaded checksum manifest using gh attestation verify SHA256SUMS --repo jasonachkar/lasa, then run sha256sum --strict -c SHA256SUMS in the directory containing all listed assets.

Azure releases instead provide SHA256SUMS.asc and release-signing-key.asc. They use an OpenPGP signature by the APT signing key; this is not a GitHub OIDC build attestation. Import the public key into a dedicated verification keyring, confirm its full primary fingerprint against your organization's trusted LASA signing fingerprint, verify gpg --verify SHA256SUMS.asc SHA256SUMS, and check the manifest hashes before installing. A key downloaded alongside a binary is not independently trusted. A valid signature proves control of the signing key, not that the builder was uncompromised.

Native package managers verify the configured repository/package trust chain automatically. Homebrew checks the archive hash pinned in its formula. Release provenance verification is an additional check for direct downloads.

docs.title: First private report
docs.text:
mkdir -m 0700 ./reports
lasa scan --format json --output ./reports/first.report.json
lasa report --input ./reports/first.report.json --format terminal
lasa report --input ./reports/first.report.json --format html --output ./reports/first.report.html

Report parents must already exist. LASA rejects symlinks in report paths and uses mode 0600 with atomic replacement. The HTML file is self-contained; it does not load fonts, scripts, images or other resources from a remote service. Protect HTML and JSON equally because both may expose infrastructure metadata.

docs.title: Narrowing collection
docs.text:
lasa scan --roots /usr/local/bin,/etc/systemd/system --max-files 2048 --timeout 20s

--roots replaces the default file roots. It does not change process or socket collection. Inspection is limited to metadata and two directory levels beneath each explicit root; it does not promise an exhaustive recursive crawl. Use separate, narrowly scoped roots for deeper relevant directories.

docs.title: Elevated and container views
docs.text:
First inspect lasa doctor and the unprivileged report. Run a deep scan only in a host context and with authorization appropriate to your organization:

sudo lasa scan --profile deep --format json --output ./reports/deep.report.json

Root-owned reports remain private to their owner. Procfs hidepid, ptrace policy, user namespaces and container restrictions can still limit root's view. An elevated scan does not certify that the entire host was observed.

Use --profile container when scanning inside a container. It reports that limited scope rather than silently presenting the result as a host audit. See operations before exposing additional host namespaces or mounts.

docs.title: Updating and uninstalling
docs.text:
Keep the binary version and report schema version in your deployment inventory. Review rule and schema changes before comparing reports from a new release. Replace the installed binary through your normal package/deployment workflow and restart a daemon after replacement. A running daemon does not reload new binaries or suppression files automatically.

To uninstall a native binary, stop and disable any installed LASA service first, then remove the binary and installed unit using your system administration workflow. Local reports and state directories are not automatically deleted; choose retention and secure disposal deliberately.

docs.title: One-shot operation
docs.text:
Prefer a scoped ordinary-user scan for initial evaluation. Record the scanner version, profile, roots, time and visibility limitations with the report. Treat finding thresholds as operational policy rather than a substitute for review.

Do not grant broad capabilities to suppress diagnostics. Check the failing operation and namespace first. A rootless container, restricted procfs mount or host ptrace policy can legitimately prevent observation. A deep profile is an explicit decision to inspect more metadata; it is not an automatic escalation feature.

docs.title: Daemon lifecycle
docs.text:
lasa daemon --state-dir /path/to/private/lasa --interval 15m --retention 96

LASA creates missing state directories without following symlinks and requires the final directory to be private. An advisory exclusive lock prevents two LASA daemons from using the same state directory. Each scheduled scan finishes before the interval timer for the next scan starts. This avoids overlapping work even when scanning takes longer than expected.

Snapshots are written as scan-TIMESTAMP-SCANID.json, with mode 0600, sync and atomic replacement. A crash can leave a hidden .lasa-*.tmp file; it is not a valid completed snapshot and is ignored by report retention. A write or retention failure is fatal to the daemon, making storage failures visible to its supervisor.

Send SIGTERM or SIGINT for graceful shutdown. An in-progress scan receives cancellation and can persist a partial result before exit. Kernel filesystem operations cannot always be interrupted promptly; configure your supervisor's stop timeout accordingly. There is no concurrent web server or remote management listener.

docs.title: Retention and capacity
docs.text:
Retention limits snapshot count. At 96 reports and a 15-minute delay, the nominal window is about a day plus scan time, but timing, restarts and errors change it. Large reports can consume substantial storage. Set disk monitoring and an external byte/time retention policy if required; Use --retention-bytes to add a managed-snapshot byte quota and --min-free-bytes to reserve space before the next report. Neither is a quota on unrelated files or a guarantee against concurrent disk exhaustion.

Only correctly named, scanner-owned regular snapshots are removed by built-in retention. Unrelated files, symlinks, locks and leftover temporary files are retained. Do not use the state directory as a general-purpose document directory. Backups and copied reports need their own access and deletion policies.

docs.title: systemd
docs.text:
Two example units are supplied:

  • lasa.service: static ordinary service account, constrained kernel/device access, empty capability set and local state directory. Visibility is intentionally limited.
  • lasa-deep.service: explicit root metadata inspection, with only read/search and ptrace capabilities listed for the relevant collection operations. It does not enable eBPF.

Example installation for the ordinary-user unit, after reviewing the file:

getent passwd lasa >/dev/null || sudo useradd --system --user-group --no-create-home --shell /usr/sbin/nologin lasa
sudo install -m 0755 bin/lasa /usr/local/bin/lasa
sudo install -m 0644 deploy/systemd/lasa.service /etc/systemd/system/lasa.service
sudo systemctl daemon-reload
sudo systemctl enable --now lasa.service
sudo journalctl -u lasa.service

Inspect the first persisted report and its coverage. The units avoid ProtectProc=invisible, ProcSubset=pid and private user namespaces, which would conceal evidence. The units intentionally leave ProtectSystem and ProtectHome disabled because read-only bind mounts would change writeability metadata and suppress relevant file permission candidates. Analysis remains read-only in the scanner code. The static service account also avoids DynamicUser state-directory symlinks, which the storage boundary rejects. Kernel/device protections can still alter their specific views. Choose host visibility and service hardening together and validate coverage on your target distribution.

The examples are deployment starting points, not verified unit compatibility on every systemd/kernel version. Neither unit is a complete sensor deployment. Sensor operation needs explicit BTF/tracefs visibility, BPF/perf permissions, memory limits and a kernel validation run described in the maintainer sensor guide.

docs.title: Container deployment
docs.text:
Build the architecture-matching binary, then the optional minimal image:

make build
docker build -f deploy/container/Dockerfile -t lasa:local .
docker run --rm --read-only --cap-drop ALL --security-opt no-new-privileges lasa:local

ARM64 hosts need the ARM64 binary. The scratch image has no shell or package manager and runs as UID 65532. Its default command declares a container view. Procfs and root filesystem content in that view differ substantially from the host; a useful container report can be partial.

Do not add --privileged, mount the entire host root or expose runtime sockets just to remove warnings. Host scanning from a container requires a separately reviewed deployment and tests for PID, user, mount and network namespaces. No privileged host-container recipe is presented as universally correct.

docs.title: Sensor windows
docs.text: lasa scan --profile sensor --sensor-duration 5s requests static scanning plus a finite metadata event window. lasa daemon --profile sensor repeats those windows on its scan schedule. This is not continuous observation: gaps exist between windows. Ring-buffer, event-retention and namespace-correlation limits appear in coverage and diagnostics. A failed attachment is not represented as successful runtime coverage.

docs.title: Operational acceptance
docs.text: Before a fleet rollout, verify useful unprivileged observations, expected privileged visibility if required, report file access, coverage policy, retention, graceful shutdown, alert delivery and the behavior of incomplete comparisons. Add representative Linux VM tests for your distributions, kernels, container runtimes and service manager. Preserve diagnostics in central ingestion so a missing permission cannot appear as a healthy host.

docs.title: Scheduling inspections
docs.text:
sudo lasa daemon --profile deep --inspect systemd,ssh,sudo,permissions,scheduler   --state-dir /var/lib/lasa --interval 15m --timeout 2m   --retention 96 --retention-bytes 1073741824 --min-free-bytes 67108864

Review the expanded collection contract and the required native providers before deployment. The example metadata-only systemd units do not automatically grant all optional inspection permissions or install native tools. Package checks additionally require a current local advisory database; schedule its refresh separately and monitor failures.

A collector fault is isolated and recorded as incomplete coverage. Fatal persistence/retention failures stop the daemon with a specific error so its process supervisor can alert/restart it. Reports are not silently discarded to make a scan appear successful. Validate shutdown, disk pressure, retained-byte limits and restart behavior under your own workload.

docs.title: Package advisories
docs.text: Package inspection compares native installed-package versions against a local, release-specific advisory database. Scanning does not download advisories or upload a package inventory. Advisory retrieval is a separate, explicit network operation.

docs.title: Update from the official Debian tracker
docs.text:
Run this on your Linux management or scanning system. Choose the exact release codename:

lasa advisories update --release trixie --output ./advisories.json
lasa scan --inspect packages --advisories ./advisories.json \
  --format json --output packages.report.json

For Debian 12, use --release bookworm. The updater downloads the official Debian Security Tracker JSON over verified HTTPS, streams source-package records, preserves fixed vendor versions and records provenance and expiry. It refuses redirects, invalid data and download/cache size limits. The endpoint does not provide a detached JSON signature; LASA does not claim signed-vendor provenance for this download.

The database expires seven days after retrieval. Schedule the updater separately from scans using your approved scheduler. A failed update does not replace an existing database. Keep the failure visible; an expired database must not silently become a clean vulnerability result.

docs.title: Other vendor-derived databases
docs.text:
Import a database that has been prepared and authenticated through your organization's vendor-data process:

lasa advisories import --input vendor-advisories.json --output ./advisories.json

Import validates structure, supported schema and freshness. It does not authenticate an arbitrary file's claimed vendor identity or convert every vendor feed format. Built-in automatic retrieval currently targets Debian; Ubuntu and supported RPM-family distributions use the documented import format.

Use the exact distribution identifier and version reported by the inspected system. Debian uses its release codename when available. Ubuntu uses ubuntu:VERSION_ID; RPM-family systems use ID:VERSION_ID from os-release, including the minor release where present. A database for a different release is not substituted.

Example synthetic database:

{
  "schema": "lasa.advisories/v1",
  "source": "https://vendor.example/security",
  "fetched_at": "2026-01-01T00:00:00Z",
  "expires_at": "2026-01-08T00:00:00Z",
  "records": [
    {
      "id": "VENDOR-EXAMPLE-001",
      "distribution": "ubuntu:24.04",
      "package": "example-service",
      "source_package": false,
      "introduced": "1.0-1",
      "fixed": "1.0-1ubuntu0.2",
      "severity": "high"
    }
  ]
}

The example is deliberately expired and does not represent a real advisory. Supply real vendor-derived timestamps and records; do not extend timestamps merely to silence expiry. Optional source_updated_at records an upstream timestamp when available. Optional uncertain: true preserves an undetermined vendor assessment instead of treating it as a confirmed affected or unaffected range.

Ranges include introduced and exclude fixed. An omitted introduced has no lower bound; an omitted fixed records an unresolved range. Supported severities are informational, low, medium, high and critical. source_package: true uses native source-package metadata where available. Preserve vendor epochs, release suffixes, security-update revisions and backport identifiers.

docs.title: Native version matching
docs.text:
Debian and Ubuntu use dpkg-style epoch/upstream/revision ordering. Supported RPM-family identifiers are rhel, rocky, almalinux, centos, fedora, ol, sles and opensuse-leap; matching uses RPM epoch/version/release ordering. Native inventory requires dpkg-query or rpm respectively.

This avoids assuming that an older-looking upstream version lacks a distribution's backported fix. Matching still depends on accurate vendor data and the package database. It does not verify every executable byte, inspect vendored application dependencies or establish exploitability. Unsupported distribution/version schemes remain unknown.

docs.title: Running-service association
docs.text:
LASA can associate an affected package with an observed process when the current executable path matches the captured device/inode metadata and the native database identifies its owner. Non-loopback listeners can then increase review priority.

Deleted, replaced, unowned, ambiguous or inaccessible executable paths remain explicit association gaps. Updating a package does not establish that every running process has restarted into the new code. Review the recorded identity and restart affected services through your operations process.

docs.title: Freshness and storage
docs.text:
--advisory-max-age defaults to 168 hours. 0 disables this additional age limit while retaining the database's own expiry check. A future fetch timestamp beyond clock tolerance, expired database, malformed file or missing release data produces a diagnostic. Known vendor uncertainty is preserved.

Cache files are written privately and atomically. They contain package/advisory data and source metadata, not scan reports. Reports store relevant installed versions, advisory identifiers, fixed versions, severity, data provenance and selected running-service relationships. They do not embed the complete advisory cache or package database.

Treat imported database producers as part of your security trust boundary. See data access and privacy and detection coverage.

docs.title: The problem LASA helps investigate
docs.text:
Linux security depends on combinations of conditions. A listener, a root process and an enabled kernel feature have very different implications depending on how they relate. LASA organizes local evidence so an operator can prioritize combinations that deserve attention: for example, a potentially reachable process that also carries powerful initial-user-namespace capabilities.

LASA is useful for host posture reviews, workload privilege reviews, pre-deployment checks, incident triage and tracking the effect of hardening changes. It is a point-in-time evidence tool, not an incident response verdict, vulnerability exploit framework, malware detector or replacement for a firewall policy review.

docs.title: What happens during a scan
docs.text:
1. LASA determines its visible Linux scope and records the time and host identity context.
  2. It collects bounded process, socket, namespace, kernel-control and explicitly scoped file metadata.
  3. It connects evidence that refers to the same visible subjects.
  4. It evaluates reviewed local rules, preserving unknown and conflicting evidence.
  5. It emits findings, supporting observations, conditional risk scenarios, coverage and diagnostics.

There is no active network reconnaissance or direct outbound discovery request during a scan. Optional native providers and advisory management have the separate access contract below. Local socket information is read from the kernel; LASA does not try connecting to each service. The optional sensor observes a finite event window and is requested explicitly through the sensor profile.

docs.title: Facts, deductions and scenarios
docs.text:
A fact might establish that a process owns a TCP listener or that a file has a particular permission mode. A deduction may associate a conventional management port with that process. A scenario explains a possible consequence if an attacker first obtains the necessary access or control.

Those are different kinds of statements. A wildcard listener is potentially reachable outside loopback, but its internet reachability is unknown. An SSH authorized-key file with permissive metadata might still be rejected by SSH. A container-looking cgroup name is a hint rather than proof of a container runtime boundary. LASA includes these qualifications in the relevant finding.

docs.title: Profiles
docs.text:
Profile Intended use Privilege behavior standard Safe baseline in the current visible Linux namespaces Ordinary user; no elevation deep Explicitly authorized higher-visibility host metadata inspection Requires effective UID 0; still subject to capabilities and policy container An explicitly acknowledged container view Does not add host access sensor Static snapshot plus a finite eBPF metadata event window Requires separately authorized kernel prerequisites; failures remain visible

Deep does not turn off security controls, connect to runtime sockets, read credentials or recursively crawl the whole filesystem. Root in a restricted container does not become host root merely by selecting a profile.

docs.title: Reading the outcome
docs.text:
Review the declared scope and collection diagnostics before interpreting findings. A scan may successfully write a useful report while some checks remain incomplete. Enable --strict when automation must distinguish this state through the process exit code.

For each finding, examine its observed evidence, prerequisites, confidence, uncertainty and recommended remediation. Verify impact and maintenance constraints before changing a production service. LASA does not execute remediation actions.

docs.title: Where the product fits
docs.text:
Reports are usable on their own, in a local operations process, or by a future SecureObs ingestion service. LASA does not require a backend, a graph database or an always-running agent to perform a one-shot scan. It does not monitor activity continuously unless an operator arranges repeated sensor windows; scheduled windows can have observation gaps.

See data and privacy, result interpretation and compatibility before deploying it fleet-wide.

docs.title: Effective configuration and advisory inspection
docs.text:
Use --inspect to add supported systemd, SSH, sudo, discretionary permissions, nftables, Docker-compatible runtime, package-advisory and scheduler checks. Modules emit evidence and coverage into the same report and finding workflow. These modules can read selected configuration/native-provider output beyond the default metadata sources; they do not run exploit tests or apply remediation.

Start with security inspections, prepare package advisories if needed, and review detection coverage. Configuration changes and advisory data remain subject to their provider and freshness requirements. A larger enabled scope is not a guarantee that every security condition can be decided.

docs.title: Start with scope and coverage
docs.text:
A report is a record of what LASA could inspect within a declared scope and resource budget. Read host.scope, profile, coverage, complete and diagnostics before interpreting its findings.

Coverage counters describe enumerated work: attempted items, successful metadata collection, skipped entries, unsupported features and inconclusive checks. They are not a percentage of all possible host vulnerabilities or all assets on a network. A process can have a successfully collected status while its descriptors remain inaccessible; therefore successful and inconclusive counts can refer to different subchecks on the same process. The counters are not interchangeable denominators.

Ordinary user scans frequently encounter permission restrictions. Missing optional kernel paths, process exits, symlink exclusions or resource limits can also result in partial coverage. LASA does not silently convert those gaps into secure conditions.

docs.title: Observation states
docs.text:
State Interpretation observed The value was obtained or a supported deduction was established not_observed A condition was evaluated and not established as present unknown Missing, inaccessible, conflicting, truncated or otherwise inadequate evidence not_applicable This check does not apply to the subject or value type

An unknown observation does not mean false. A rule requiring unknown evidence does not produce a confirmed match. Reports preserve rule evaluation outcomes so the absence of a finding can be distinguished from an evaluated negative result.

docs.title: Three independent risk dimensions
docs.text:
Severity describes the rule's potential consequence: informational, low, medium, high or critical. Confidence describes the evidence and inference: confirmed, high, medium, low or unknown. Builtin findings currently use high or medium confidence; LASA does not label an inferred compromise scenario confirmed. Exposure describes reachability evidence:

  • confirmed: independently verified exposure evidence; static collection does not produce this state.
  • potential: a non-loopback endpoint, including wildcard bindings, was observed.
  • local: the endpoint is loopback or UNIX-local; this is not a blanket statement about other relay/proxy paths.
  • unknown: reachability could not be established for the subject.

IPv6 wildcard bindings do not establish that IPv4 traffic will be accepted. LASA does not infer dual-stack policy or upstream reachability from a bind address. Optional firewall inspection adds a separately qualified local nftables verdict; it does not establish upstream NAT, cloud security-group or load-balancer policy.

docs.title: What a finding contains
docs.text:
A finding includes a fingerprint, versioned rule identity, affected subject, severity/confidence/exposure, supporting observation references, prerequisites, a conditional scenario, uncertainties, remediation and a transparent priority score. Related process instances can share a stable finding identity; their evidence is retained rather than treated as separate scan executions.

Use lasa explain to inspect the recorded evidence. No explanation proves that compromise occurred. A remediation is advice to review, not an action LASA executes. For example, enabling a seccomp mode may require workload-specific testing and does not by itself establish that a useful attack surface was removed.

docs.title: Priority scores
docs.text:
The current score is a bounded 0–100 prioritization index. Each finding exports the scoring version and named contributions. It combines rule consequence, exposure evidence and observed initial-user-namespace privilege. It is not a probability, compliance score or estimate of successful exploitation.

LSM presence and enabled seccomp do not automatically earn risk reductions: configuration presence alone does not prove an effective mitigation. Compare priorities within the documented scoring version; changing a rule or score version can change a finding's meaning.

docs.title: Conditional scenarios and attack paths
docs.text:
The report connects observed relationships such as process ownership of a listener and possession of a capability. Any step requiring compromise, write access not fully proven, a later service restart or a particular upstream policy remains conditional. LASA does not invent a missing vulnerability to turn adjacent facts into an exploit chain.

Current correlations are local evidence combinations centered on a subject. They are not an enterprise-wide lateral movement simulation or a proof that every listed graph neighbor forms one executable sequence.

docs.title: Comparing snapshots
docs.text:
lasa diff old.report.json new.report.json requires matching host identities. It classifies findings as new, continuing, materially changed, resolved or unknown. Material changes include priority, severity, confidence, exposure, suppression status and supporting evidence.

A missing finding is only marked resolved when its relevant evidence collectors have complete coverage, the recorded profile/scope is compatible, and there is an explicit negative/not-applicable rule evaluation for the same stable subject. Disappearing or unenumerated assets remain unknown. This conservative policy can require a follow-up scan before a dashboard can claim resolution. Broader file roots or a different profile also affect comparability; record scan scope alongside reports.

Fingerprint stability favors service identity, executable and stable cgroup context rather than PID alone. A resource rename, host identity change, container replacement or rule version change can legitimately yield a new fingerprint. A missing machine ID forces a boot-scoped fallback and is diagnosed; it weakens continuity across reboots.

docs.title: Suppressions
docs.text:
Suppression acknowledges a reviewed finding without removing its evidence. Create a local JSON file:

{
  "schema": "lasa.suppressions/v1",
  "entries": [
    {
      "fingerprint": "REPLACE_WITH_FULL_FINDING_FINGERPRINT",
      "justification": "Temporary exception approved under change SEC-123; compensating controls verified by owner.",
      "expires": "2026-12-01T00:00:00Z"
    }
  ]
}

Apply with --suppressions exceptions.json. A unique fingerprint and nonempty justification are mandatory; expiration is optional. Expired entries no longer suppress. Suppressed data stays in reports and SARIF exports, but does not trigger --fail-on. Protect and review this file as security policy; the daemon loads it at startup, so restart after a change.

docs.title: Report formats
docs.text: JSON is the complete versioned interchange form. Terminal output is a readable summary and displays a bounded diagnostic preview; JSON retains every diagnostic. HTML is a static self-contained report containing observations and actionable errors. SARIF 2.1.0 uses genuine logical resource locations for runtime findings rather than fabricated source-code filenames. Some GitHub code scanning views require repository physical locations and may omit or poorly display host findings; retain the JSON/HTML report as the operational record.

docs.title: Report and diff versions
docs.text:
New scans emit lasa.report/v2. The extension records inspection assets, enabled modules, requested metadata roots and a scope fingerprint; default scans still keep the baseline collection scope. The saved-report renderer accepts legacy lasa.report/v1 without inventing inspection data. Older scanner builds and external consumers must be upgraded before consuming v2. Inspection extensions cannot be mislabeled as v1.

lasa diff emits lasa.diff/v2, including bounded surface_changes and an explicit changes_truncated flag. See detection coverage for inventory-change and resolution semantics. Public schemas are available for v2 and the legacy v1 contract.

Legacy reports without a scope fingerprint cannot establish compatible collection scope for automatic resolution; absent findings remain unknown until comparable v2 baselines are available.

docs.title: Current integration boundary
docs.text:
LASA is independently usable. It requires no SecureObs credentials, APIs, database or frontend. The integration artifact is the local JSON snapshot with schema lasa.report/v2. No automatic upload or background remote transmission is implemented.

A SecureObs-side adapter can ingest authorized reports from a controlled file transfer, deployment agent or ingestion service. That adapter owns authentication, transport, tenant authorization, encryption, retention and audit logging. Never infer authorization from the report's host ID alone.

docs.title: Recommended ingestion contract
docs.text:
Preserve schema, scanner_version, scan_id, scan times, profile and host identity. Treat scan_id as the execution identity and the finding fingerprint as cross-scan issue identity. Preserve evidence references, observation state, provenance, confidence, exposure, prerequisites, scoring version and contributions, suppressions, coverage and diagnostics.

Ingest each (tenant, authorized_asset_mapping, scan_id) idempotently. Map the pseudonymous LASA host ID to an asset only through an authenticated inventory process. Container images cloned with the same machine ID can collide operationally; a host hash is not proof of asset identity.

Do not mark an issue resolved merely because a later report omits it. Preserve unknown and partial outcomes. LASA's diff output uses lasa.diff/v1 and can guide this behavior, but the backend still needs policy for profiles, collection scope and rule/score-version transitions.

docs.title: Safe ingestion
docs.text:
Validate size and schema before storage. Restrict nesting and array counts, reject unsupported versions, preserve referential integrity and escape all displayed strings. JSON is data, never executable queries or template code. Do not make network requests to socket addresses, file paths, schema URIs or other strings found in a report.

For downstream code scanning integrations, SARIF exports logical runtime locations. GitHub repository views can have limited support for those locations; do not invent source-file coordinates to make a host finding appear inline.

The public report JSON schema documents the exported field contract. Preserve schema versioning independently of the executable version.

Ingestion must recognize v2 inspection assets and module/scope metadata. Legacy v1 remains readable by the current CLI, but older consumers are not automatically v2-compatible. Preserve unknowns, actual evidence dependencies, surface-change truncation and advisory freshness; do not convert lost visibility into resolution.

docs.title: Security inspections
docs.text: LASA combines its default Linux metadata scan with optional configuration inspections. Use these inspections to connect service settings, local identities, execution paths, container configuration and package advisories to evidence-backed findings.

docs.title: Choose the collection scope
docs.text:
A default lasa scan retains its metadata-only behavior. Configuration inspection is an explicit choice:

lasa scan --inspect systemd,ssh,permissions --format json --output inspection.report.json

Enable all inspection modules when you have authorization for their documented access:

sudo lasa scan --profile deep --inspect all --advisories advisories.json \
  --timeout 2m --max-inspection-items 1024 \
  --format json --output inspection.report.json

LASA never elevates itself. sudo is an operator choice; --profile deep requires effective UID 0. Inspection flags also work with lasa daemon. Modules are independent of the base profile: --inspect all enables every module, while a container profile continues to describe the container-visible system.

--roots controls the baseline filesystem metadata collector. It does not restrict the configuration providers enabled by --inspect. Those providers use the sources described below. Review data access and privacy before enabling them.

If lasa scan --help does not list --inspect, update to a scanner build containing inspection modules. New scans use report schema v2; see results and compatibility.

docs.title: What each module checks
docs.text: Module Inspected sources Findings and qualifications systemd Loaded and enabled service inventory; selected effective system-manager properties Writable root-service executables, interpreter scripts and environment-file paths; selected missing restrictions on an associated root listener. Effective overrides come from the manager. Alternate root images/directories and unsupported execution syntax remain unknown. ssh Configuration-only sshd -G output for selected connection contexts Root password authentication without a required additional method; disabled StrictModes. These describe policy for the recorded context, not a successful login, unlocked account or reachable SSH service. sudo Local passwd/group metadata and noninteractive native long-list policy queries Unrestricted root delegation, passwordless unrestricted grants and writable delegated command paths. Native policy evaluation handles configuration includes and aliases; unsupported output/RunAs expressions remain unknown. Intended administrator grants can be suppressed with a justification and expiry. permissions Selected privileged/sensitive paths, their ancestry, ownership, ACLs and mount metadata Named local identities with discretionary write or replacement candidates. This supplements baseline permission-bit findings; it does not attempt a write. firewall JSON nftables rules in the scanner network namespace; observed listeners and interface addresses Management endpoints permitted by the supported nftables packet model. Verdicts cover a recorded packet context and do not prove upstream reachability. containers An explicitly selected local Docker-compatible UNIX socket, through read-only HTTP queries Running privileged containers, host PID mode, runtime socket mounts, sensitive writable bind mounts and selected dangerous-capability/unconfined combinations. The selected daemon defines the runtime scope. packages Native installed-package database, selected executable ownership queries and a local advisory database Distribution-specific affected versions, high-severity advisories and affected packages associated with non-loopback listeners. Vendor backport versions are compared with Debian/RPM semantics. scheduler System crontab, /etc/cron.d, root crontab spool locations and active systemd timers Writable execution/configuration/search paths in supported root jobs and timer services. Shell expansion, pipelines, wrappers and other unsupported syntax produce coverage diagnostics.

docs.title: Systemd execution and permissions
docs.text:
Systemd inspection queries effective properties instead of treating every unit-looking file as an active service. It considers loaded active/activating services and enabled/linked service configurations. A disabled, inactive unit is not automatically treated as an active root entry point.

For supported interpreters, LASA identifies the script path as well as the interpreter. Supported relative scripts use the effective working directory. Environment-file paths and permissions are inspected; their contents are not opened by LASA. Inline programs and unsupported execution options remain explicit gaps. A privileged command prefix in a non-root unit requires independent review.

A discretionary access candidate can involve writing a file directly or replacing an affected path component. LASA considers local UID/group membership, ACL masks, directory search permission, sticky-directory ownership, read-only mount state and mount boundaries. It detects selected metadata changes during inspection and asks for a rerun when the path changes.

The result remains conditional: immutable/append-only flags, SELinux/AppArmor policy, remote filesystem authorization, service activation and later changes can affect actual impact. External directory-service membership and arbitrary identity-provider policy are not reconstructed from /etc/passwd and /etc/group.

docs.title: SSH connection contexts
docs.text:
sshd -G requires OpenSSH 9.3 or later. LASA uses configuration-only mode rather than host-key validation mode. An unavailable provider produces a diagnostic; it does not fall back to reading private keys.

Supply representative contexts so Match conditions are evaluated for intended clients:

sudo lasa scan --inspect ssh \
  --ssh-context 'user=root,host=admin.example,addr=192.0.2.20,laddr=192.0.2.10,lport=22' \
  --ssh-context 'user=deploy,host=admin.example,addr=192.0.2.20,laddr=192.0.2.10,lport=22' \
  --format json --output ssh.report.json

Required context fields are user, host, addr, laddr and lport; rdomain is optional. Addresses must be IP literals. The default context is root from localhost to localhost on port 22. A result for that default is not a statement about every remote client. Context values are stored in the report.

docs.title: Firewall packet contexts
docs.text:
For a wildcard listener, supply a destination address actually observed on a local interface. Supply source and interface information when policy depends on them:

sudo lasa scan --inspect firewall \
  --network-source 192.0.2.20 \
  --network-destination 192.0.2.10 \
  --network-interface eth0 \
  --format json --output firewall.report.json

The model considers new TCP/UDP traffic, supported literal address/prefix/port/interface conditions, inline sets/ranges, base-chain policy and supported chain jumps/returns. Later base chains can still block an earlier accept. An empty nftables input policy does not establish filtering.

Unsupported expressions, named sets, packet transformations, other hooks or insufficient packet context produce an unknown verdict. Legacy iptables, XDP/tc, upstream firewalls, NAT, cloud security groups and application authentication are outside this verdict. Other network namespaces require independent inspection. LASA does not send a packet or make an authentication attempt to establish these findings.

docs.title: Container runtime access
docs.text:
sudo lasa scan --inspect containers --container-socket /run/docker.sock \
  --format json --output containers.report.json

This module uses a Docker-compatible API, versions 1.24 through 1.50, over the selected UNIX socket. It does not implement containerd's native gRPC API or the Kubernetes API. Compatible Podman endpoints must implement the queried Docker API behavior. Remote TCP endpoints and redirects are not used.

Runtime socket access is privileged even when LASA sends only read-only requests. A read-only bind mount of a UNIX socket does not restrict its API operations. Inspect responses can contain environment values and other sensitive fields in transit through scanner memory; LASA discards those fields and stores only its selected configuration evidence. This access is excluded from the default scan.

docs.title: Budgets, failures and unknowns
docs.text:
--max-inspection-items defaults to 256 and accepts 1–4096. It bounds enumerated work within each module, including permission targets. Command output, API responses, file reads, evidence arrays and report exports have additional bounds. A limit produces incomplete coverage rather than a claim that remaining assets are safe.

--inspection-command-timeout defaults to 5 seconds per native command. --timeout bounds the whole scan cooperatively. Native command cancellation terminates its process group. A kernel-blocked filesystem operation can still require external process supervision; no in-process timeout can guarantee interruption of every kernel operation.

Inspect inspect.MODULE coverage and diagnostics before accepting a report. Missing tools, missing permissions, inaccessible managers/sockets, unsupported syntax, stale advisories and timeouts identify the affected operation and scope. Raw native error output is withheld when it could contain configuration secrets; recognized errors retain safe cause and configuration-location information.
